# Round 36 — The UMW covering: six constructive strategies, 15 adversarial verdicts, ZERO coverings. The door is confirmed OPEN-and-HARD.

A multi-strategy constructive attack on the one standing door — the Umans–Wang
(arXiv:2511.10851) `(α,β)=(1/3,1/3)` divisibility-covering of `[n]`, which would imply
deterministic integer factoring `1/5 → 1/6`. Each strategy was **built and run** in
python3/sympy with a known-answer harness, then **attacked by two adversarial verifiers**
that independently re-ran the harness to check the guards.

## Verdict: NO `(1/3,1/3)` covering was constructed — and none was disproved either

**15/15 adversarial verdicts: `is_real_covering = False`.** Several verifiers forced
headline retractions of the runs' own over-claims ("the headline must be retracted", "not
even an attempt at the target regime"). **Zero real coverings.** The door is neither opened
nor rigorously closed this round — it is confirmed **open-and-hard**.

Strategies attempted: multi-scale difference cover; smooth-number (factor-base) differences;
prime-power/valuation-structured; interval/Cantor-style structured `S,T`; a full covering
built from many Lemma-6.2 primorial APs; and a lower-bound proof attempt.

## What is now rigorously established about the door
- **The tightness at `(1/3,1/3)` is open in BOTH directions.** Proving achievability yields
  factoring `1/6` (a major result); proving impossibility would disprove the tightness of a
  published conjecture (also major). The paper itself: *"we do not know if `α = 1−2β` is
  achievable."* Neither is known.
- **Empirical frontier (main loop, disjoint-guarded greedy, coverage over ALL of `[n]`
  including composites):** full coverage `1.00` only at the traded point `(α,β)=(1/2, 2/3)`;
  at the target `(1/3,1/3)` greedy reaches only `0.40–0.54` (rising with n). Unstructured
  search is far from the target — consistent with UMW requiring a **structured** `S,T`.
- **The α-unit subtlety (a real experimental trap):** the magnitude bound is
  `magnitude ≤ exp(n^α)`, so `α` is a **double-exponential** parameter; the measured `α` from
  a construction with max element `M` is `ln ln M / ln n`, **not** `ln M / ln n`. Any covering
  experiment computing `α` the latter way measures a different quantity.
- **UMW's three conflatable statements, disambiguated (verified at source):** the abstract's
  trivial boundary `α+β ≤ 1+o(1)`; the counting **constraint** `α ≥ 1−2β` (the binding one);
  and the trivial covering `α = 1−β+o(1)`. At `β=1/3` the constraint floor is `α=1/3`
  (zero slack) while the trivial point is `α=1−β=2/3`; **the gap between them is the entire
  open content.**

## Honest status
Zero new factoring methods, as in every prior round. But this round **strengthens the
negative** on the standing door: it is not a soft opening — six distinct construction
families fail at the target, the empirical frontier is `(1/2, 2/3)`, and the remaining
question (tightness of `α ≥ 1−2β` at `1/3,1/3`) is a known-hard open problem in both
directions. Combined with the capstone (the deterministic barrier is motif-intrinsic; every
term-level escape inside the Lehman–BSGS motif is exhausted), the campaign's frontier is
narrow, well-characterised, and honestly at its limit for classical deterministic methods.

# Closing the Galois-table completeness gap: AGL(1,8) has the LARGEST abelianization examined and leaks the LEAST — extending the semiprime REVERSAL

The `semiprime_reversal` (D₄ 1.43 bits > S₄ 1 bit) showed the semiprime splitting-type
channel is driven by coset SEPARATION, not group size. That raised a completeness question:
the catalog machine-checked only groups with `|G^ab| ≤ 4` (S₃, S₄, A₄, D₄, V₄, C₄), so the
cap-headroom above 2 bits was **entirely untested**. This note computes the first case with
`|G^ab| > 4` — and it **reverses the reversal**.

## AGL(1,8) = GF(8) ⋊ GF(8)× , order 56
- Derived subgroup `[G,G]` = the translation group `C₂³` (order 8) — verified normal.
- Abelianization `G^ab = C₇` (order 7), **cap = log₂7 = 2.807 bits** — the largest
  abelianization of any group examined.
- Type readout `T(g)` = cycle type of `g` as a permutation of the 8 field points;
  **verified to be a class function** (conjugation-invariant, 200 random checks).

**Computed exactly over all 3136 = 56² ordered pairs (x,y):**
- Prime channel `I₁ = I(coset(x); T(x)) = 0.5917 bits` — only **21.1%** of the cap.
- **Semiprime channel `I₂ = I(coset(xy); {Tx,Ty}) = 0.1141 bits` — only 4.1% of the cap.**

(Consistency: `0 ≤ I₂ ≤ I₁ ≤ cap`, as required.)

## The extended reversal
| group | order | \|G^ab\| | cap | I₂ (semiprime) | % of cap realized |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| V₄ | 4 | 4 | 2.00 | 0.295 | 14.7% |
| **AGL(1,8)** | **56** | **7** | **2.807** | **0.114** | **4.1%** |
| S₄ | 24 | 2 | 1.00 | 1.000 | 100% |
| D₄ | 8 | 4 | 2.00 | 1.430 | 71.5% |

(Values for V₄, S₄, D₄ are the catalog's machine-checked closed forms, `Semiprime.lean`.)

⇒ **Having the LARGEST abelianization (7) gives the SMALLEST semiprime leakage (0.114) of any
group examined.** So the channel richness is not merely "not monotone in group size" (the
original D₄>S₄ reversal) — it is **not monotone in the abelianization order either**. What
matters is how much of `G^ab` the class-function type readout `T` actually RESOLVES: D₄'s `T`
resolves 71.5% of its 2-bit cap; AGL(1,8)'s `T` resolves only 4.1% of its 2.807-bit cap.
Large abelianization with a **coarse** (lossy) class function is a *worse* channel than a small
one with a faithful class function.

## Why it matters (and what it does NOT claim)
- It **completes the machine-checked table's headroom** (the first `|G^ab| > 4` case) and
  makes the "coset separation drives leakage" reading precise: it is **separation as resolved
  by `T`**, i.e. `I(coset;T)`, not `log₂|G^ab|` alone.
- It does **NOT** threaten factoring: `I₂` is a bounded (O(1)-per-fixed-field) number of bits
  about a residue of `N`, versus Θ(log N) needed to localise `p`; and per the harvest (#420)
  the family lands on existing primitives (1)/(4) — real mechanism, wrong quantity.
- The structural lemma it instantiates: `I(coset;T) = log₂|G^ab| − H(coset|T)`, so the deficit
  `H(coset|T)` (the `loss_eq` of `GroupChannel.lean`) is what varies wildly across groups, and
  it is maximised exactly when `T` is a coarse class function on a large abelian quotient.

Computed with python3/sympy, exact rationals, all `G×G` enumerated; the derived subgroup and
class-function property were verified in code, not assumed.

  rw [agl8_prime_loss]

  rw [agl8_prime_channel, l6_eq]
  have := l3_gt; have := l3_lt; have := l7_gt; have := l7_lt
  constructor <;> linarith

of the `log₂ 7` cap. -/

    (0.2107 : ℝ) < mutualInfo aglSet aglCoset aglType / entropy aglSet aglCoset ∧

  rw [agl8_prime_channel, agl8_cap, l6_eq]
  have := l3_gt; have := l3_lt; have := l7_gt; have := l7_lt
  have hp : (0 : ℝ) < logb 2 7 := by linarith
  constructor
  · rw [lt_div_iff₀ hp]; linarith
  · rw [div_lt_iff₀ hp]; linarith

/-- **The affine-ladder collapse.**  The catalog's `abelianization_law_degree_seven`
(`Bridges.AffineFrobeniusLadderAGL7`) gives `AGL(1,7)` — abelianization `C₆`, cap `log₂ 6` —

transmits less than a third of that.  Channel size is *anti*-correlated with the cap along the
affine ladder. -/

    logb 2 6 < entropy aglSet aglCoset ∧
    3 * mutualInfo aglSet aglCoset aglType < 1 / 3 + logb 2 3 := by
  rw [agl8_cap, agl8_prime_channel, l6_eq]
  have := l3_gt; have := l3_lt; have := l7_gt; have := l7_lt
  constructor <;> linarith
